key_terms.meaning: Straight line on the output characteristic joining V_CE = V_CC (cut-off) and I_C = V_CC/(R_C + R_E) (saturation); any possible Q-point lies on it.
The fixed DC values (I_CQ, V_CEQ) the transistor sits at when no signal is applied.
S = dI_C/dI_CO, the change in collector current caused by a unit change in the reverse saturation current; a small S means a steady Q-point.
Rise in temperature raises I_C, which raises power dissipation and temperature again, until the device is destroyed.
Base resistor R_B from V_CC sets I_B = (V_CC − V_BE)/R_B; simple, but I_C = β·I_B follows β directly.
R_B is returned to the collector, so negative feedback through R_B partly holds I_C steady when β changes.
R1–R2 fix V_B, R_E fixes V_E, and I_C ≈ (V_B − V_BE)/R_E is nearly independent of β.
An unbypassed R_E gives DC negative feedback, so I_C moves only slightly with β or temperature.
The line V_GS = −I_D·R_S drawn on the transfer characteristic; its crossing with the device curve is the FET Q-point.
Drain current at V_GS = 0 and the pinch-off gate voltage; both datasheet values are needed to place a JFET Q-point.
Two-port small-signal model using h_ie (input resistance), h_re (reverse voltage feedback), h_fe (forward current gain) and h_oe (output admittance).
Physical small-signal model with r_π = β/g_m, a dependent source g_m·v_be, output resistance r_o = V_A/I_CQ, and capacitances C_π and C_μ.
Model with r_e = V_T/I_E = α/g_m in the emitter leg and a controlled source α·i_e in the collector leg.
The voltage at which the extrapolated output curves meet the V_CE axis; r_o ≈ V_A/I_CQ.
Common-collector stage: gain just under 1, no phase inversion, high input resistance, low output resistance.
Small-signal drain current per volt of gate-source signal; g_m = √(2k_n·I_D) = 2I_D/V_OV for a MOSFET.
Common-drain stage with the drain grounded for signals; gain just under 1 and input resistance set only by the gate resistors.
A capacitor between stages passes the signal but blocks DC, so each stage keeps its own Q-point while low-frequency gain falls.
CE stage stacked on a CB stage; the CB stage holds the CE collector almost fixed, removing the Miller effect and widening bandwidth.
Emitter of the first BJT drives the base of the second; current gain ≈ β1·β2 and input resistance ≈ β1·β2·R_E.

takeaways: The DC load line fixes the set of allowed operating points; biasing means choosing one that stays put.
A good bias network makes I_C depend on resistor values and V_BE, not on β.
The voltage divider with an emitter resistor is preferred because its stability factor is the smallest of the simple circuits.
A FET is biased by voltage, not current, so its Q-point is found graphically on the transfer characteristic.
The h-parameter, hybrid-π and T models describe the same transistor and must give the same answers.
CE gives voltage gain with inversion; CB gives current gain with no inversion; CC gives voltage gain near 1 and a low output resistance.
Because the gate draws no current, a CS amplifier can have an input resistance in the megohms without any special design.
Multistage coupling decides everything: RC coupling isolates DC, transformer coupling matches impedance, direct coupling passes DC.
The cascode trades a second transistor for bandwidth; the Darlington trades two base-emitter drops for current gain.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a circuit diagram, a derivation, and a numerical Q-point or gain — draw the circuit first, mark every current and voltage, then substitute numbers with units.

bank.q: Explain the DC load line of a CE amplifier. Mark cut-off, saturation and a typical Q-point on it, and explain what happens to the Q-point when temperature rises.
outline: Draw the output characteristic family with the load line from V_CE = V_CC to I_C = V_CC/(R_C + R_E)
Define the Q-point and show the mid-point choice for maximum swing
State that I_CO and V_BE both rise with temperature, so I_C rises and the Q-point moves towards saturation
Mention the shift of the load line itself if R_C changes with temperature

bank.q: Define bias stabilization and the stability factor S. Derive S for fixed bias and for voltage divider bias, and compare the two values.
outline: Define S = dI_C/dI_CO with I_B, β and V_BE held constant
Fixed bias: S = 1 + β, very poor
Voltage divider: I_C ≈ (V_B − V_BE)/R_E, giving S well below 1 + β; quote S ≈ (1+β)(1 + R_B/R_E)/(1+β+R_B/R_E)
Show the general rule S = (1+β)/(1 + β·R_E/(R_B + R_E))
Say why small S is wanted

bank.q: Compare fixed bias, collector-to-base feedback bias and voltage divider bias on Q-point stability, number of resistors, input resistance and suitability for production.
outline: Circuit of each with the formula for I_C
Fixed bias: fewest parts, S = 1 + β, I_C depends on β
Collector feedback: negative feedback through R_B, moderate improvement
Voltage divider: best stability, costs two resistors and a bypass capacitor
Input resistance: highest for voltage divider, lowest for fixed bias

bank.q: Explain how a self-bias line is drawn on the transfer characteristic of a JFET and how the Q-point and I_D are obtained from it.
outline: Write V_GS = −I_D·R_S
Plot it as a straight line through the origin with slope −1/R_S
Shockley curve: I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)²
Intersection gives I_DQ and V_GSQ
Also mention the V_DD − I_D(R_D + R_S) load line on the output curves

bank.q: Describe the h-parameter model of a BJT in CE configuration. Define each parameter, give its typical magnitude and its units.
outline: Two-port equations v_be = h_ie·i_b + h_re·v_ce and i_c = h_fe·i_b + h_oe·v_ce
h_ie in ohms, h_re dimensionless, h_fe dimensionless, h_oe in siemens
Typical values: h_ie ≈ 1 kΩ, h_fe ≈ 100, h_oe ≈ 25 µS, h_re ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁴
Measurement condition: output shorted for h_ie and h_fe; input open for h_re and h_oe
Relation h_fe = β and h_ie = r_π

bank.q: A silicon BJT has β = 100, V_CC = 15 V, R_B = 470 kΩ and R_C = 3.3 kΩ in fixed bias. Find I_B, I_C, V_CE and comment on the location of the Q-point.
outline: I_C = β·I_B ≈ 3.04 mA
V_CE = V_CC − I_C·R_C ≈ 5.0 V
Check V_CE > 0.3 V, so the device is in active region
Note that I_C changes almost one-for-one with β

bank.q: Design a voltage divider bias for a CE stage with V_CC = 12 V, I_C = 2 mA, V_CE = 6 V and β = 150. Use the design rules V_E ≈ 0.1·V_CC and I_R2 = 10·I_B, then find the new Q-point when β doubles.
outline: V_E = 1.2 V, so R_E = 0.6 kΩ; V_C = V_CE + V_E = 7.2 V, so R_C = 2.4 kΩ
With β = 300 the change in I_C is only a few per cent because I_C ≈ (V_B − V_BE)/R_E

bank.q: Using the hybrid-π model, derive the voltage gain, input resistance and output resistance of a CE amplifier with a bypassed emitter resistor and a load R_L.
outline: Draw the model with r_π, g_m·v_be and r_o
v_be = v_i because the emitter is bypassed to ground
A_v = −g_m(r_o ∥ R_C ∥ R_L)
R_i = R_B ∥ r_π
R_o = r_o ∥ R_C; state that the gain is negative, so the stage inverts

bank.q: An emitter follower with β = 100, r_π = 2 kΩ and R_E = 1 kΩ is driven from a source of resistance R_s = 10 kΩ and feeds a 1 kΩ load. Find the voltage gain and the output resistance.
outline: Conclude: no inversion, gain near unity, output resistance in tens of ohms

bank.q: A MOSFET with k_n = 1 mA/V² and V_t = 1 V is biased with R_D = 2 kΩ, R_S = 1 kΩ and a gate divider giving V_G = 3 V, with V_DD = 10 V. Find I_D, V_DS and g_m.
outline: V_GS = V_G − I_D·R_S and I_D = k_n(V_GS − V_t)²
Solve the quadratic to get I_D ≈ 1 mA and V_GS = 2 V
V_DS = V_DD − I_D(R_D + R_S) = 7 V, so saturation holds
V_OV = V_GS − V_t = 1 V, g_m = 2I_D/V_OV = 2 mS
Check I_D against the data-sheet parameter if given

bank.q: Compare RC coupling, transformer coupling and direct coupling for multistage amplifiers on voltage gain, bandwidth, DC level shifting, size and cost. State one application for each.
outline: RC coupling: simple, cheap, wide band, poor low-frequency response, DC blocked
Transformer coupling: good impedance matching and efficiency, bulky and costly, poor high-frequency response
Direct coupling: passes DC, used in op-amp and audio IC stages, but Q-point drift propagates
Gain in dB adds: A_total = A1·A2·A3
Applications: RC in audio preamps, transformer in RF and power stages, direct in op-amps

bank.q: A three-stage RC-coupled amplifier has stage gains of 20, 15 and 10, with each stage having f_L = 100 Hz and f_H = 100 kHz. Find the overall gain in dB and discuss how the overall cut-off frequencies relate to those of the individual stages.
outline: A_total = 20 × 15 × 10 = 3000, that is 69.5 dB
Each stage contributes a pole; the overall lower cut-off moves higher than 100 Hz
The overall upper cut-off moves lower than 100 kHz
Bandwidth therefore shrinks as stages are added, roughly as 1/√(2^(1/n) − 1) times the single-stage value
State the gain-bandwidth trade-off

bank.q: Explain the cascode amplifier. Derive its voltage gain and show why its bandwidth is far larger than that of a single CE stage with the same gain.
outline: Circuit: CE transistor with a CB transistor stacked above it
Gain ≈ −g_m1·R_L, the same as a CE stage, but the CB stage holds the CE collector nearly fixed
Miller capacitance is (1 + A_v)C_μ in a plain CE stage; in the cascode the first stage sees a gain near −1
Input pole therefore moves to a much higher frequency
Costs: extra supply headroom and a second bias branch

bank.q: Explain the Darlington pair. Derive its current gain, input resistance and effective base-emitter voltage, and state the drawbacks.
outline: Emitter of Q1 drives base of Q2; I_C ≈ β1·β2·I_B1
R_i ≈ β1·β2·R_E, which is why it is used as a buffer
V_BE(total) ≈ 1.4 V, so the input must rise by two diode drops
Drawbacks: leakage current is also multiplied by β, slower turn-off, higher saturation voltage
Use: series regulator pass element, audio output stage, touch sensors

glossary.def: A straight line drawn on the device characteristic showing every (voltage, current) pair allowed by the external resistors.
The DC collector current and collector-emitter voltage of a transistor when the signal is zero.
Setting the DC currents and voltages of a device so that it sits in the active region before any signal arrives.
The rate at which collector current changes when the reverse saturation current changes, with β and V_BE fixed.
Self-heating that increases current, which increases heating again, ending in device failure.
The state where the transistor carries almost no current because the input junction is not forward biased.
The state where the transistor is fully on and V_CE has fallen to a small value such as 0.2 V.
A capacitor placed across R_E so that AC signal current bypasses the resistor while DC bias still flows through it.
A capacitor between two stages that passes the signal but blocks DC, so each stage keeps its own Q-point.
One of four hybrid two-port numbers (h_ie, h_re, h_fe, h_oe) describing a transistor for small signals.
Forward current gain in CE, equal to β; about 100 for a small-signal BJT.
The small-signal change in output current divided by the change in input voltage that causes it; unit siemens.
Small-signal BJT model built from r_π, a controlled current source g_m·v_be, r_o and the junction capacitances.
Small-signal model that places r_e = V_T/I_E in the emitter lead and a current source α·i_e in the collector lead.
The extrapolated voltage V_A at which the BJT output curves meet the axis; it sets r_o = V_A/I_C.
The signal amplitude is small enough that the device behaves linearly about its Q-point.
The resistance seen looking into the amplifier input; it decides how much the source is loaded.
The resistance seen looking back into the amplifier output; it decides how far the gain drops under load.
Common-collector amplifier whose output at the emitter follows the input with gain just below one.
Common-drain FET amplifier whose output at the source follows the gate input.
CE stage stacked on a CB stage to reduce Miller effect and increase bandwidth.
Two cascaded emitter followers giving a current gain equal to the product of the two β values.
A circuit that copies a reference current into another branch using matched transistors.
Joining two stages through a capacitor and a resistor so that the signal passes but DC does not.
